      <content name="title">Heart <span class="qt3">Failure</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">CHF</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cardiac <span class="qt3">Failure</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Congestive Heart <span class="qt3">Failure</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Low Cardiac Output</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Left-sided heart <span class="qt3">failure</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Right-sided heart <span class="qt3">failure</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>?<p>Heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> means that your heart can't pump enough oxygen-rich blood to meet your body's needs. Heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> doesn't mean that your heart has stopped or is about to stop beating. But without enough blood flow, your organs may not work well, which can cause serious problems.</p><p>Heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> can affect one or both sides of your heart:</p><ul><li>With right-sided heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>, your heart is too weak to pump enough blood to your lungs to get oxygen.</li><li>With left-sided heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>, your heart can't pump enough oxygen-rich blood out to your body. This happens when the left side of your heart becomes either:
	<ul><li>Too weak to pump enough blood.</li><li>Too thick or stiff to relax and fill with enough blood.</li></ul></li></ul><p>Left-sided heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> is more common than right-sided heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>.</p>What causes heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>?<p>Heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> can start suddenly after a medical condition or injury damages your heart muscle. But in most cases, heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> develops slowly from long-term medical conditions.</p><p>Conditions that can cause heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> include:</p><ul><li>Arrhythmia (a problem with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat)</li><li>Cardiomyopathy</li><li>Congenital heart defects or other types of heart diseases that you are born with</li><li>Coronary artery disease</li><li>Endocarditis</li><li>Heart attack</li><li>Heart valve diseases</li><li>High blood pressure</li><li>A blood clot in your lung</li><li>Diabetes</li><li>Certain severe lung diseases, such as COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)</li><li>Obesity</li></ul><p>Over time, left-sided heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> can lead to right-sided heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>.</p>Who is more likely to develop heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>?<p>Heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> can happen at any age. It happens to both men and women, but men often develop it at a younger age than women.  Your chance of developing heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> increases if:</p><ul><li>You're 65 years old or older. Aging can weaken and stiffen your heart muscle.</li><li>Your family health history includes relatives who have or have had heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>.</li><li>You have changes in your genes that affect your heart tissue.</li><li>You have habits that can harm your heart, including:
	<ul><li>Smoking</li><li>Eating foods high in fat, cholesterol, and sodium (salt)</li><li>Having an inactive lifestyle</li><li>Alcohol use disorder (AUD)</li><li>Illegal drug use</li></ul></li><li>You have other medical conditions that can affect your heart, including: 
	<ul><li>Any heart or blood vessel conditions, including high blood pressure</li><li>Serious lung diseases</li><li>Infection, such as HIV or COVID-19</li><li>Obesity</li><li>Diabetes</li><li>Sleep apnea</li><li>Chronic kidney disease</li><li>Anemia</li><li>Thyroid disease</li><li>Iron overload disease</li><li>Cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span> that can harm your heart, such as radiation and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">chemotherapy</span></span></span></li></ul></li><li>You are African American. African Americans are more likely to develop heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> and have more serious cases at younger ages than people of other races. Factors such as stigma, discrimination, income, education, and geographic region can also affect their risk of heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>?<p>The symptoms of heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> depend on which side of your heart is affected and how serious your condition has become.  Most symptoms are caused by reduced blood flow to your organs and fluid buildup in your body.</p><p>Fluid buildup happens because the flow of blood through your heart is too slow. As a result, blood backs up in the vessels that return the blood to your heart. Fluid may leak from the blood vessels and collect in the tissues of your body, causing swelling (edema) and other problems.</p><p>Symptoms of heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> may include:</p><ul><li>Feeling short of breath (like you can't get enough air) when you do things like climbing stairs. This may be one of the first symptoms you notice.</li><li>Fatigue or weakness even after rest.</li><li>Coughing.</li><li>Swelling and weight gain from fluid in your ankles, lower legs, or abdomen (belly).</li><li>Difficulty sleeping when lying flat.</li><li>Nausea and loss of appetite.</li><li>Swelling in the veins of your neck.</li><li>Needing to urinate (pee) often.</li></ul><p>At first you may have no symptoms or mild symptoms. As the disease gets worse, your symptoms will usually bother you more.</p>What other problems does heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> cause?<p>Fluid buildup and reduced blood flow to your organs can lead to serious problems, including:</p><ul><li>Breathing problems from fluid in and around your lungs (also called congestive heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>)</li><li>Kidney or liver damage, including cirrhosis</li><li>Malnutrition if fluid buildup makes eating uncomfortable or if your stomach doesn't get enough blood flow to digest food properly</li><li>Other heart conditions, such as irregular heartbeat and sudden cardiac arrest</li><li>Pulmonary hypertension</li></ul>How is heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>, your health care provider will</p><p> 
</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history, including your symptoms</li><li>Ask about your family health history, including relatives who have had heart <span class="qt3">failure</span></li><li>Do a physical exam</li><li>Likely run heart tests and blood tests, including a brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) test</li></ul><p>In some cases, your provider may refer you to a cardiologist (a doctor who specializes in heart diseases) for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p>What are the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span> for heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>?<p>Your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> will depend on the type of heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> you have and how serious it is. There's no cure for heart <span class="qt3">failure</span>. But <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> can help you live longer with fewer symptoms.</p><p>Even with <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>, heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> usually gets worse over time, so you'll likely need <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> for the rest of your life.</p><p>Most <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> plans include:</p><ul><li>Taking medicine</li><li>Eating less sodium and drinking less liquid to control fluid buildup</li><li>Making other changes, such as quitting smoking, managing stress, and getting as much physical activity as your provider recommends</li><li>Treating any conditions that may make heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> worse</li></ul><p>You may need heart surgery if:</p><ul><li>You have a congenital heart defect or damage to your heart that can be fixed.</li><li>The left side of your heart is getting weaker and putting a device in your chest could help. Devices include:
	<ul><li>An implantable cardioverter defibrillator.</li><li>A biventricular pacemaker (cardiac resynchronization <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span>).</li><li>A mechanical heart pump (a ventricular assist device (VAD) or a total artificial heart).</li></ul>
</li><li>Your heart doctor recommends a heart transplant because your heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> is life-threatening and nothing else is helping.</li></ul><p>As part of your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>, you'll need to pay close attention to your symptoms, because heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> can worsen suddenly. Your provider may suggest a cardiac rehabilitation program to help you learn how to manage your condition.</p>Can heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> be prevented?<p>You may be able to prevent or delay heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> if you:</p><ul><li>Work with your provider to manage any health conditions that increase your risk of developing heart <span class="qt3">failure</span></li><li>Make healthy changes in your eating, exercise, and other daily habits to help prevent heart disease</li></ul><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Respiratory <span class="qt3">Failure</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">ARDS</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span>?<p>Respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span> is a condition in which your blood doesn't have enough oxygen or has too much carbon dioxide. Sometimes you can have both problems.</p><p>When you breathe, your lungs take in oxygen. The oxygen passes into your blood, which carries it to your organs. Your organs, such as your heart and brain, need this oxygen-rich blood to work well.</p><p>Another part of breathing is removing the carbon dioxide from the blood and breathing it out. Having too much carbon dioxide in your blood can harm your organs.</p>What causes respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span>?<p>Conditions that affect your breathing can cause respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span>. These conditions may affect the muscles, nerves, bones, or tissues that support breathing. Or they may affect the lungs directly. These conditions include:</p><ul><li>Diseases that affect the lungs, such as COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), cystic fibrosis, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, and COVID-19</li><li>Conditions that affect the nerves and muscles that control breathing, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), muscular dystrophy, spinal cord injuries, and stroke
</li><li>Problems with the spine, such as scoliosis (a curve in the spine). They can affect the bones and muscles used for breathing.</li><li>Damage to the tissues and ribs around the lungs. An injury to the chest can cause this damage.</li><li>Drug or alcohol overdose</li><li>Inhalation injuries, such as from inhaling smoke (from fires) or harmful fumes</li></ul>What are the symptoms of respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span>?<p>The symptoms of respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span> depend on the cause and the levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in your blood.</p><p>A low oxygen level in the blood can cause shortness of breath and air hunger (the feeling that you can't breathe in enough air). Your skin, lips, and fingernails may also have a bluish color. A high carbon dioxide level can cause rapid breathing and confusion.</p><p>Some people who have respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span> may become very sleepy or lose consciousness. They also may have arrhythmia (irregular heartbeat). You may have these symptoms if your brain and heart are not getting enough oxygen.</p>How is respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span> diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider will diagnose respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span> based on:</p><ul><li>Your medical history</li><li>A physical exam, which often includes</li><ul><li>Listening to your lungs to check for abnormal sounds</li><li>Listening to your heart to check for arrhythmia</li><li>Looking for a bluish color on your skin, lips, and fingernails</li></ul><li>Diagnostic tests, such as</li><ul><li>Pulse oximetry, a small sensor that uses a light to measure how much oxygen is in your blood. The sensor goes on the end of your finger or on your ear.</li><li>Arterial blood gas test, a test that measures the oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in your blood. The blood sample is taken from an artery, usually in your wrist.</li></ul></ul><p>Once you are diagnosed with respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span>, your provider will look for what is causing it. Tests for this often include a chest x-ray. If your provider thinks you may have arrhythmia because of the respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span>, you may have an EKG (electrocardiogram). This is simple, painless test that detects and records your heart's electrical activity.</p>What are the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span> for respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span>?<p><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatment</span></span></span> for respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span> depends on:</p><ul><li>Whether it is acute (short-term) or chronic (ongoing)</li><li>How severe it is</li><li>What is causing it</li></ul><p>Acute respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span> can be a medical emergency. You may need <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> in intensive care unit at a hospital. Chronic respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span> can often be treated at home. But if your chronic respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span> is severe, you might need <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> in a long-term care center.</p><p>One of the main goals of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> is to get oxygen to your lungs and other organs and remove carbon dioxide from your body. Another goal is to <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treat</span></span></span> the cause of the condition. <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatments</span></span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>Oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span>, through a nasal cannula (two small plastic tubes that go in your nostrils) or through a mask that fits over your nose and mouth</li><li>Tracheostomy, a surgically-made hole that goes through the front of your neck and into your windpipe. A breathing tube, also called a tracheostomy, or trach tube, is placed in the hole to help you breathe.</li><li>Ventilator, a breathing machine that blows air into your lungs. It also carries carbon dioxide out of your lungs.</li><li>Other breathing <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span>, such as noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV), which uses mild air pressure to keep your airways open while you sleep. Another <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> is a special bed that rocks back and forth, to help you breathe in and out.</li><li>Fluids, often through an intravenous (IV), to improve blood flow throughout your body. They also provide nutrition.</li><li>Medicines for discomfort</li><li><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatments</span></span></span> for the cause of the respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span>. These <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span> may include medicines and procedures.</li></ul><p>If you have respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span>, see your health care provider for ongoing medical care. Your provider may suggest pulmonary rehabilitation.</p><p>If your respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span> is chronic, make sure that you know when and where to get help for your symptoms. You need emergency care if you have severe symptoms, such as trouble catching your breath or talking. You should call your provider if you notice that your symptoms are worsening or if you have new signs and symptoms.</p><p>Living with respiratory <span class="qt3">failure</span> may cause fear, anxiety, depression, and stress. Talk <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">therapy</span></span></span>, medicines, and support groups can help you feel better.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/kidneyfailure.html">
      <content name="title">Kidney <span class="qt3">Failure</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">ESRD</content>
      <content name="altTitle">End-Stage Renal Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Renal <span class="qt3">Failure</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Healthy kidneys clean your blood by removing excess fluid, minerals, and wastes. They also make hormones that keep your bones strong and your blood healthy. But if the kidneys are damaged, they <span class="qt3">don't work</span> properly. Harmful wastes can build up in your body. Your blood pressure may rise. Your body may retain excess fluid and not make enough red blood cells. This is called kidney <span class="qt3">failure</span>.</p><p>If your kidneys <span class="qt3">fail</span>, you need <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> to replace the work they normally do. The <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> options are dialysis or a kidney transplant. Each <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> has benefits and drawbacks. No matter which <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> you choose, you'll need to make some changes in your life, including how you eat and plan your activities. But with the help of health care providers, family, and friends, most people with kidney <span class="qt3">failure</span> can lead full and active lives.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hearttransplantation.html">
      <content name="title">Heart Transplantation</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A heart transplant removes a damaged or diseased heart and replaces it with a healthy one. The healthy heart comes from a donor who has died. It is the last resort for people with heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> when all other <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span> have failed. The heart <span class="qt3">failure</span> might have been caused by coronary heart disease, damaged heart valves or heart muscles, congenital heart defects, or viral infections of the heart.</p><p>Although heart transplant surgery is a life-saving measure, it has many risks. Careful monitoring, <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>, and regular medical care can prevent or help manage some of these risks.</p><p>After the surgery, most heart transplant patients can return to their normal levels of activity. However, fewer than 30% return to work for many different reasons.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hepatitisc.html">
      <content name="title">Hepatitis C</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">HCV</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is hepatitis C?<p>Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver. Inflammation is swelling that happens when tissues of the body are injured or infected. Inflammation can damage organs.</p><p>There are different types of hepatitis. One type, hepatitis C, is caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV). Hepatitis C can range from a mild illness lasting a few weeks to a serious, lifelong illness.</p><p>Hepatitis C can be acute or chronic:</p><ul><li>Acute hepatitis C is a short-term infection. The symptoms can last up to 6 months. Sometimes your body is able to fight off the infection and the virus goes away. But for most people, an acute infection leads to chronic infection.</li><li>Chronic hepatitis C is a long-lasting infection. If it is not treated, it can last for a lifetime and cause serious health problems, including liver damage, cirrhosis (scarring of the liver), liver cancer, and even death.</li></ul>How is hepatitis C spread?<p>Hepatitis C spreads through contact with the blood of someone who has HCV. This contact may be through:</p><ul><li>Sharing drug needles or other drug materials with someone who has HCV. In the United States, this is the most common way that people get hepatitis C.</li><li>Getting an accidental stick with a needle that was used on someone who has HCV. This can happen in health care settings.</li><li>Being tattooed or pierced with tools or inks that were not sterilized after being used on someone who has HCV.</li><li>Having contact with the blood or open sores of someone who has HCV.</li><li>Sharing personal care items that may have come in contact with another person's blood, such as razors or toothbrushes.</li><li>Being born to a mother with HCV.</li><li>Having unprotected sex with someone who has HCV.</li></ul><p>Before 1992, hepatitis C was also commonly spread through blood transfusions and organ transplants. Since then, there has been routine testing of the U.S. blood supply for HCV. It is now very rare for someone to get HCV this way.</p>Who is more likely to get hepatitis C?<p>You are more likely to get hepatitis C if you:</p><ul><li>Have injected drugs</li><li>Had a blood transfusion or organ transplant before July 1992</li><li>Have hemophilia and received clotting factor before 1987</li><li>Have been on kidney dialysis</li><li>Have been in contact with blood or infected needles at work</li><li>Have had tattoos or body piercings</li><li>Have worked or lived in a prison</li><li>Were born to a mother with hepatitis C</li><li>Have HIV</li><li>Have had more than one sex partner in the last 6 months</li><li>Have had a sexually transmitted infection (STI)</li><li>Are a man who has had sex with men (MSM)</li></ul><p>If you are at high risk for hepatitis C, your health care provider will likely recommend that you get tested for it.</p>What are the symptoms of hepatitis C?<p>Most people with hepatitis C have no symptoms. Some people with acute hepatitis C do have symptoms within 1 to 3 months after they are exposed to the virus. These symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Dark yellow urine</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Fever</li><li>Gray- or clay-colored stools</li><li>Joint pain</li><li>Loss of appetite</li><li>Nausea and/or vomiting</li><li>Pain in your abdomen (belly)</li><li>Jaundice (yellowish eyes and skin)</li></ul><p>If you have chronic hepatitis C, you probably will not have symptoms until it causes complications. This can happen decades after you were infected. For this reason, hepatitis C screening is important, even if you have no symptoms.</p>What other problems can hepatitis C cause?<p>Without <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>, hepatitis C may lead to cirrhosis, liver <span class="qt3">failure</span>, and liver cancer. Early diagnosis and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span> of hepatitis C can prevent these complications.</p>How is hepatitis C diagnosed?<p>Providers diagnose hepatitis C based on your medical history, a physical exam, and blood tests.</p><p>If you do have hepatitis C, you may need additional tests to check for liver damage. These tests may include other blood tests, an ultrasound of the liver, and a liver biopsy.</p>What are the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatments</span></span></span> for hepatitis C?<p><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatment</span></span></span> for hepatitis C is with antiviral medicines. They can cure the disease in most cases.</p><p>If you have acute hepatitis C, your provider may wait to see if your infection becomes chronic before starting <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">treatment</span></span></span>.</p><p>If your hepatitis C causes cirrhosis, you should see a doctor who specializes in liver diseases. <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Treatments</span></span></span> for health problems related to cirrhosis include medicines, surgery, and other medical procedures. If your hepatitis C leads to liver <span class="qt3">failure</span> or liver cancer, you may need a liver transplant.</p>Can hepatitis C be prevented?<p>There is no vaccine for hepatitis C. But you can help protect yourself from hepatitis C infection by:</p><ul><li>Not sharing drug needles or other drug materials.</li><li>Wearing gloves if you have to touch another person's blood or open sores.</li><li>Making sure your tattoo artist or body piercer uses sterile tools and unopened ink.</li><li>Not sharing personal items such toothbrushes, razors, or nail clippers.</li><li>Using a latex condom during sex. If your or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>
